title: How Russia Is Attacking the Midterms with a Mother Jones Deepfake

reading.body:
This is an impersonation failure at the point of publication. A fabricated video was made to look like the output of an established news outlet, using that outlet's logo and attributed quotes from its editor, and it was distributed through social media accounts rather than through any system the outlet controls. The false claim at the centre of it, that a political party paid a named broadcaster to promote gender transition among children, was asserted as reporting.

Catching it required the platform to act on the outlet's complaint, which it did only partially, removing one post on trademark grounds. Nothing in the reporting shows that the platform's own systems detected the fabrication before the complaint, or that the view counts were verified as human. Researchers describe bot-like signals in the accounts and the counts, which means the apparent audience is itself in question.

The operation is reported to have spread other synthetic videos of public figures and fake news reports about candidates. The reporting states its reach so far has been limited, and that is a description of current distribution, not of the technique's effectiveness.

It is not established that the named individuals said or did what the videos attribute to them, that the platform's removals were complete, or that any government body investigated the network.

reports.title: How Russia Is Attacking the Midterms with a Mother Jones Deepfake

summary:
A Russian disinformation network called Matryoshka, also known as Storm-1679, has circulated a fake Mother Jones video claiming the Democratic National Committee paid $259 million to CNN chief Mark Thompson to promote gender transition among children. The video used a false Mother Jones logo and fake quotes from editor Clara Jeffery. It drew about 155,000 views on one X account and 50,000 on another. Researchers say the accounts and view counts show signs of bot activity.

The campaign also includes deepfakes of celebrities like Sarah Jessica Parker and Julia Roberts urging votes for Republicans, plus fake CNN and other news reports about Democratic candidates. Mother Jones complained to X, which removed one post for a trademark violation. The article says the operation has not gained much reach so far, but warns it could grow because the Trump administration has closed government units that tracked Russian disinformation.
